messages.subject: problem with shrink.tree?
messages.body_plain:
Dear s-news users,

Please help me with my predicament. I am using S-Plus 4.5 for 
Windows, Prof. edition, release 2.

My dataset has 500 observations. I did a regression tree with 9 
variables, using tree(). I have then done 100 10-fold cross-validations 
with cv.tree() to obtain the "best" tree size. I then use the value of k 
that comes up the most often in my cross-validations to shrink back my 
tree, using shrink.tree(mytree, k=0.31). However, whether I use that 
value of k=0.31 that I obtained with my cross-validations, or, to see 
what happens, values of k=0.9 or k=0.1, I get the same tree every time.  
It's the same as my original tree that was not shrunk.  How could that 
be?

My only sources of information are the S-Plus online manuals and 
Chambers and Hastie (1993).

Thank you,

Isabelle Robichaud
irobichaud at myrealbox.com

messages.body_plain:

I would like to ask something which for some of you maybe will

messages.subject: Re: Stepwise and significance
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 01 Aug 2002 17:09:05 +0300
Theodore Kypreos <kypreost at yahoo.gr> wrote:

> Dear s-plus users,
> 
> I would like to ask something which for some of you maybe will be easy.
> 
> As I have understood, function stepAIC (Venables and Ripley) does the 
> following. You begin from a "full" model and then the "best" model, is the 
> model which has the smallest AIC. 
> 
> 1. Is it make sense to look at the p-values of the variables, since the 
> criterion which has been used is AIC and not the significant level?

The significance levels are not very meaningful whether you use AIC or P-values 
to derive the model.  Stepwise variable selection invalidates the estimate of 
sigma, confidence limits, P-values, and to some extent the regression 
coefficient estimates.

Also, it is my understanding that AIC was developed to compare exactly two 
models.  Comparing more than two models can result in problems with inference 
and overfitting.

Frank Harrell

>

> backward and forward method, where the final model will conclude only 
> statistically significant (p-value< alpha) variables?

messages.subject: Re: Stepwise and significance
messages.body_plain:
Theodore Kypreos asks:

>   -----Original Message-----
> From: Theodore Kypreos
>   [mailto:kypreost at yahoo.gr]
> Sent: Friday, August 02, 2002 12:09
>   AM
> To: s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject: [S]
>   Stepwise and significance
>
>
>
>   Dear s-plus users,
>
>
>
>   I would like to ask something which for some of you maybe
>   will be easy.
>
>
>
>   As I have understood, function stepAIC (Venables and Ripley)
>   does the following. You begin from a "full" model and then the "best" model,
>   is the model which has the smallest AIC.
> [WNV] Not necessarily.  You can begin with any model,
>   provided it is a sub-model of the "upper" model and it contains the "lower"
>   model as a sub-model, (where "upper" and "lower" are specified in the scope
>   argument).  stepAIC attempts to find the model with lowest AIC, but
>   only through a greedy sequence, that is, at each stage it
>   either adds or omits that term, for which the change reduces the value of AIC
>   by the greatest amount.  Since the direction is always down the
>   process is guaranteed to converge, but not necessarily to find the model
>   with minimum AIC.  It is best to check the process by starting at several
>   different initial models.
>
>
>
>   1. Is it make sense to look at the p-values of the
>   variables, since the criterion which has been used is AIC and not the
>   significant level?
> [WNV] It make sense to look at
>   them, but not to believe them.  There is no allowance in them for the
>   selection effect, which will usually be severe.  Many people
>   would regard them as providing a kind of relative importance ranking, though,
>   nevertheless.  I'm not so sure that even this is altogether safe,
>   though.
>
>
>
>   2. Is it possible to do a stepwise regression which is a
>   combination of the backward and forward method, where the final model will
>   conclude only statistically significant (p-value< alpha)
>   variables?
> [WNV] If that is your wish, but not with
>   stepAIC.  You can do this kind of thing manually if you like using
>   dropterm and addterm from the MASS library.  (See the "test"
>   argument.)  Following on from 1, however, do not believe that a
>   p-value of 0.049 necessarily indicates significance at the 5% level!
>   Selection effects will wreck this.
>
>
>
>   Many thanks in advance,
>
>
>
>   Theodore

Thanks to Alan Zaslavsky and Patrick Burns who both suggested using setdiff on 
lists of function names.  The following works:

 remove(list=setdiff(objects(),objects(classes="function")))

(I believe that the argument to objects is 'type' in another version of S+ that 
I use.)

Alan also noted that it is good practice to keep important objects somewhere 
other than the working directory.

Thanks

Robert

messages.subject: Re: remove all data objects
messages.body_plain:
Robert Burbridge asks:

>  -----Original Message-----
> From:         Burbidge, Robert [mailto:robert.burbidge at csfb.com] 
> Sent: Thursday, August 01, 2002 10:27 PM
> To:   's-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu'
> Subject:      [S] remove all data objects
> 
> Hi,
> 
> I'm new to S+.  I'm using v6.1 professional trial edition, on windows NT.
> 
> This may sound dumb: when running scripts, how do I clear all data
> objects?
        [WNV]  What do you mean by "data" objects?  This is a highly
ambiguous term and not everyone shares your view.  Sorry to be picky but
this is the nub of your problem.

> I've tried:
> 
> remove(list=objects())
> 
> but that deletes everything in the working directory, including functions.
> There's obviously:
> 
> remove(list=objects(type="numeric"))
> remove(list=objects(type="matrix"))
> remove(list=objects(type="data.frame"))
> ....
        [WNV]  actually obviously not, because objects( ) does not have a
type= argument.

> but that's plainly absurd.
        [WNV]  Right.  Suppose you want to remove just the matrices, data
frames and numeric vectors:

                toGo <- c("matrix", "data.frame", "numeric")
                remove(objects(classes = toGo))

        There's a pattern there that I'll leave you to intuit.  Now suppose
you want to remove everything but the functions:

                remove( setdiff(objects( ), objects(classes = "function")) )
        or
                remove( setdiff(objects( ), c(objects(classes = "function"),
"toGo", "thisAndThat") )

        if you don't want some particular non-functions to disappear.

        The other tack you can take is to open the objects explorer (I can't
believe I'm actually saying this, <shudder>) click on the objects you don't
want and press delete.  Well some people do it.

        Bill Venables.

> tia

messages.subject: Wilcoxon test
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to compare predicted and observed mean parasite data,  using
Wilcoxon test as the data is not normally distributed. I run tests from a
script, and they are of the following format:

expa9 <- valdata[,"expa9"]
meana <- valdata[,"meanA"]
ad.test <- wilcox.test(expa9, meana, alternative = "two.sided", paired="T")
ad.test$p.value

which occasionnally returns:
"Warning messages:
cannot compute exact p-value with ties in: wil.sign.rank(dff, alternative,
exact, correct)"
SPlus actually does return a p value - Does anybody know what kind of amount
of error I am dealing with in the p value? can I somewhat trust the p value
returned, or not at all? Otherwise, is there a way to force it to handle
ties in data?

My second question is more general: SPlus does not do Wilcoxon tests on
large datasets (n>25) - what is the alternative when  data is not normally
distributed, and n>25?

Thanks a lot!

Helene

messages.subject: Re: Wilcoxon test
messages.body_plain:
I think you are overly concerned about `not normally distributed'.  Your
data are not from the assumptions of the Wilcoxon test either.  But then
as you are using paired=T you are actually using a signed rank test on the
differences, and its assumptions are also violated.

The signed rank test assumes independent samples from a continuous
symmetric distribution, and tests that the point of symmetry is 0.
There cannot be ties.

The two-sample paired t test is pretty robust to non-normality, and I
suggest you use that if you really need a test.  However, plots are
likely to be more revealing.  For n < 25 you will only be able to detect
gross departures (and only of difference in mean).

On Fri, 2 Aug 2002 msc0235 at geo.ed.ac.uk wrote:

> I am trying to compare predicted and observed mean parasite data,  using
> Wilcoxon test as the data is not normally distributed. I run tests from a
> script, and they are of the following format:
>
> expa9 <- valdata[,"expa9"]
> meana <- valdata[,"meanA"]
> ad.test <- wilcox.test(expa9, meana, alternative = "two.sided", paired="T")
> ad.test$p.value
>
> which occasionnally returns:
> "Warning messages:
> cannot compute exact p-value with ties in: wil.sign.rank(dff, alternative,
> exact, correct)"
> SPlus actually does return a p value - Does anybody know what kind of amount
> of error I am dealing with in the p value? can I somewhat trust the p value
> returned, or not at all? Otherwise, is there a way to force it to handle
> ties in data?

To the last, no, as the distribution for non-continuous distributions
depends on the distribution.  So-called `distribution-free' tests are
only so for continuous distributions.

> My second question is more general: SPlus does not do Wilcoxon tests on
> large datasets (n>25) - what is the alternative when  data is not normally
> distributed, and n>25?

Not so.  S-PLUS does do these tests for n > 25: it just uses an
approximation to the p-values.  Given that the assumptions made are
not tenable, I would not worry about the approximation of the p values.

--

messages.subject: Random number generation in S
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I am interested in generating random numbers from a positive stable
distribution for alpha (the stability parameter) = 1/2.  I am able to do
this based on the formula (Eq.2.2) given in Chambers et al. (1976, JASA).
There is also an easier method due to Brown and Tukey, which yields the
required random numbers as the reciprocal of the square of standard normal
deviates.  However, I don't know how to best ascertain the quality of the
random deviates, i.e. do the simulated random numbers satisfy the necessary
mathematical properties?

This led me to think about the quality of random numbers generated by SPlus,
in general.  Other than simple mean, variance, histogram, etc., are there
powerful diagnostic tools to check the quality of random numbers? For
example, how can I check that the results of "rnorm" are indeed std. normal?
Also, how can I find out about the algorithms used in Splus to generate
various types of random numbers? They seemed to be implemented as internal
functions.  For example, the documentation for "rnorm" says that the
standard normal deviates are calculated based on the ratio of uniform
deviates.  In this method, the number of uniform deviates per normal deviate
is about 2.74.  Why is the simpler "Box-Mueller" method not implemented,
which uses only 2 uniform deviates per normal deviate?

thanks for the help,
Ravi Varadhan.

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, 4 Aug 2002, Ravi Varadhan wrote:

> I am interested in generating random numbers from a positive stable
> distribution for alpha (the stability parameter) = 1/2.  I am able to do
> this based on the formula (Eq.2.2) given in Chambers et al. (1976, JASA).
> There is also an easier method due to Brown and Tukey, which yields the
> required random numbers as the reciprocal of the square of standard normal
> deviates.  However, I don't know how to best ascertain the quality of the
> random deviates, i.e. do the simulated random numbers satisfy the necessary
> mathematical properties?
>
> This led me to think about the quality of random numbers generated by SPlus,
> in general.  Other than simple mean, variance, histogram, etc., are there
> powerful diagnostic tools to check the quality of random numbers? For
> example, how can I check that the results of "rnorm" are indeed std. normal?

E.g. a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on a large sample gives a p value, and on
repeated runs that p-value should be uniform (which can be tested by
another KS test).  But empirical testing can never be particularly
powerful, and in particular in most applications it is much more important
to have independence of successive samples than normality.

> Also, how can I find out about the algorithms used in Splus to generate
> various types of random numbers? They seemed to be implemented as internal
> functions.

The only available information is on the help pages.  Why do you want to
know?  Do you know how your computer implements sin() for example?

> For example, the documentation for "rnorm" says that the
> standard normal deviates are calculated based on the ratio of uniform
> deviates.  In this method, the number of uniform deviates per normal deviate
> is about 2.74.  Why is the simpler "Box-Mueller" method not implemented,
> which uses only 2 uniform deviates per normal deviate?

It's `Box-Muller', not `Box-Mueller'.  There are well-known deficiencies of
that method, including speed (sin, cos, log are all fairly slow) and undue
sensitivity to the PRNG used.

You can find the answers to all your questions in good books on simulation.
Be aware though that most of the literature uses `random numbers' to mean
samples from U(0,1).

--

messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "Jacob" == Jacob van Wyk <jlvw at rau.ac.za> writes:

    Jacob> Could anybody please help: I simply want to generate
    Jacob> random samples from a multinomial distribution with
    Jacob> fixed n and given probability vector p.

    Jacob> How can I do this?

I've recently written the following {for the R package "normix"}.  
The above is really a FAQ.
I think I'd propose to adopt this (or an improvement of it) both
for R and S-plus :

  ## This is based on rmultz2() from S-news by Alan Zaslavsky & Scott Chasalow
  ## {and adapted from the R package "combinat"}.
  ## Arg.names like  rbinom();  returns  n x p matrix

  rmultinom <- function(n, size, prob) {
      K <- length(prob) # #{classes}
      matrix(tabulate(sample(K, n * size, repl = TRUE, prob) + K * 0:(n - 1),
                      nbins = n * K),
             nrow = n, ncol = K, byrow = TRUE)
  }

messages.subject: Re: Random number generation in S
messages.body_plain:
I would like to thank Prof. Ripley and Bert Gunter for their replies.
However, my primary question on how to compare the two methods for
generating pseudo-random numbers from a positive-stable ditsribution, with
alpha=1/2,  still remains. The results from these two methods are quite
different (in terms of the moments and histograms), even for large numbers
of random deviates (say, 10,000 or 100,000).  I recognize that the
distribution from which I am simulating doesn't have finite moments.  So I
am wondering how to compare the two methods (Chambers et al. 1976, JASA, Eq.
2.2,  and Brown and Tukey's method).

Also, it is hard for me to believe that with the mathematical coprocessors
being so advanced these days that the computation of sin(), cos() , and
log() functions would be slower than calling a uniform pseudo-random number
generator.  May be this would be one of the reasons why should know a little
more about the computer implementation of elementary functions.

Thanks once again,
Ravi.

----- Original Message -----
From: "Prof Brian D Ripley" <ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk>
To: "Ravi Varadhan" <rvaradha at jhsph.edu>
Cc: <s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu>
Sent: Monday, August 05, 2002 3:31 AM
Subject: Re: [S] Random number generation in S

> On Sun, 4 Aug 2002, Ravi Varadhan wrote:
>
> > I am interested in generating random numbers from a positive stable
> > distribution for alpha (the stability parameter) = 1/2.  I am able to do
> > this based on the formula (Eq.2.2) given in Chambers et al. (1976,
JASA).
> > There is also an easier method due to Brown and Tukey, which yields the
> > required random numbers as the reciprocal of the square of standard
normal
> > deviates.  However, I don't know how to best ascertain the quality of
the
> > random deviates, i.e. do the simulated random numbers satisfy the
necessary
> > mathematical properties?
> >
> > This led me to think about the quality of random numbers generated by
SPlus,
> > in general.  Other than simple mean, variance, histogram, etc., are
there
> > powerful diagnostic tools to check the quality of random numbers? For
> > example, how can I check that the results of "rnorm" are indeed std.
normal?
>
> E.g. a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on a large sample gives a p value, and on
> repeated runs that p-value should be uniform (which can be tested by
> another KS test).  But empirical testing can never be particularly
> powerful, and in particular in most applications it is much more important
> to have independence of successive samples than normality.
>
> > Also, how can I find out about the algorithms used in Splus to generate
> > various types of random numbers? They seemed to be implemented as
internal
> > functions.
>
> The only available information is on the help pages.  Why do you want to
> know?  Do you know how your computer implements sin() for example?
>
> > For example, the documentation for "rnorm" says that the
> > standard normal deviates are calculated based on the ratio of uniform
> > deviates.  In this method, the number of uniform deviates per normal
deviate
> > is about 2.74.  Why is the simpler "Box-Mueller" method not implemented,
> > which uses only 2 uniform deviates per normal deviate?
>
> It's `Box-Muller', not `Box-Mueller'.  There are well-known deficiencies
of
> that method, including speed (sin, cos, log are all fairly slow) and undue
> sensitivity to the PRNG used.
>
> You can find the answers to all your questions in good books on
simulation.
> Be aware though that most of the literature uses `random numbers' to mean
> samples from U(0,1).
>
> --

S-News readers,

I would like to perform some simulations to evaluate the performance of the significance tests of the fixed effects from models fitted using the gls() function in the NLME library. Specifically, I am interested in assessing the marginal significance of the fixed effect predictors when a spatial correlation structure is included in the overall model specification. As implemented, the tests are ordinary t-tests that are produced via the summary() function. I want to simulate realizations of the original fitted model by systematically assigning each of the predictors a value of zero to be consistent with the null hypothesis, and I would appreciate some suggestions on how to efficiently do this step of the simulation. messages.subject: assigning names and values
messages.body_plain:
I received several responses to my question about dummy coding one
variable with 8 levels in 20 different data sets.  I thank Paul Lin,
Alan Zaslavsky, Nick Ellis, Steven McKinney, Sam Buttrey, and Burt
Gunter for their help.  I have included the responses below.  For those
interested, I have place my question is near the bottom of the message.

#-----Paul Lin------------------
You can do this via for loops.  Say the data names are "df1", ...,
"df20", the score variable is appropriately named "score", and we want
to create "dummy1", ..., "dummy7" with score=8 as baseline group:

dataset.names <- paste("df", 1:20, sep="")
dummy.names <- paste("dummy", 1:7, sep="")
for (dataset.name in dataset.names) {
    df <- get(dataset.name)
    for (i in 1:7) {
        dummy.name <- dummy.names[i]
        df[,dummy.name] <- ifelse(df$score==i, 1, 0)
    }
    assign(dataset.name, df, where=1, immediate=T)
}

I suppose you can also use eval(parse()) to do without use of "df".  As
a trade off, the code would be much less readable.

#---------Alan Zaslavsky-----------------------
I am assuming that these are data.frames and the variable you are
startin 
with is a numeric (with integer values in 1:8). If the imputed variable
is "blah", and the list of datasets is in dslist, try

for(dsname in dslist) {
  ds_get(dsname)
  ds$blah <- contr.treat(8)[ds$blah,]
  assign(dsname,ds)
  }

#--------Nick Ellis-----------------------------
convert the variable into a factor, select the kind of contrast you want
and use model.matrix to get the dummy variables. E.g.:

 fac <- rep(1:8,each=3)
 fac <- as.factor(fac)
 contrasts(fac) <- contr.treatment(levels(fac))
 model.matrix(~fac)

#-----Steven McKinney------------------------------------
Here's a way to do it using the S-PLUS modeling machinery
used in functions such as glm, mle etc.

> foo <- data.frame(y = runif(20), x =  runif(20), g =
> as.factor(sample(8,
size = 20, rep = T)))
> bar <- model.frame(~ g - 1, foo)
> baz <- model.matrix( ~ g - 1, bar, contrasts = list(g =
> contr.treatment)) baz
   g1 g2 g4 g5 g6 g7 g8
1  0  1  0  0  0  0  0
2  0  0  0  0  1  0  0
3  1  0  0  0  0  0  0
4  0  0  0  0  1  0  0
5  0  0  0  1  0  0  0
6  1  0  0  0  0  0  0
7  0  0  0  1  0  0  0
8  0  0  0  0  0  0  1
9  0  1  0  0  0  0  0
10  0  0  0  0  0  0  1
11  1  0  0  0  0  0  0
12  0  0  0  0  0  0  1
13  0  0  1  0  0  0  0
14  0  0  0  0  0  0  1
15  0  0  0  1  0  0  0
16  0  0  0  0  0  1  0
17  0  0  0  0  0  1  0
18  0  1  0  0  0  0  0
19  0  0  0  0  1  0  0
20  0  0  0  0  0  1  0
>

The resulting design matrix (baz) can be used for dummy coded variables.
Using contr.treatment will get you 0-1 indicator codings.  For a factor
with 8 levels, you can pick 7 columns of the above design matrix (leave
out the column corresponding to the factor level you want to use as the
baseline group). Using contr.sum will get you a design matrix that will
yield coefficient estimates that sum to zero, as is common in much ANOVA
modeling.

#--------Bert Gunter------------------------------
see contrasts().
(As you probably already know by now)

It is probable that you don't (didn't) need to do this, however, as the
S language modeling function generally take care of this automatically,
unlike SAS.

#--------Sam Buttrey-------------------
Try this. First make sure that the relevant variable is a factor; then
use model.matrix() to do the work. For example:

# Create the data
> frank <- data.frame (x = 1:20, y = rnorm (20), z = sample (1:7, size =

> 20, replace=T)) frank$z <- as.factor (frank$z)
#
# Set "treatment" contrasts
#
> options(contrasts = rep ("contr.treatment", 2))
#
# Run like the wind!
#
> model.matrix (~ . - 1, data = frank)

tree() in Splus is *not* written by Prof. Ripley, but by Pregibon & Clark,
as documented in the "white book" (Statistical Models in S).  Prof. Ripley
tried to patch some problems in the original code, and wrote the "tree"
package for R (see http://r-project.org).  "tree" and "rpart" mainly differ
in the tree splitting criterion: rpart uses node impurity (as measured by
Gini index); tree uses deviance.  "rpart" does surrogate splits; "tree"
doesn't.  Handling of missing values are also different between the two.
See the chapter in the white book or the tech report bundled with "rpart"
for details.  BDR himself (and several others) advocate use of rpart over
tree.

For bagging, there are a couple of packages for R: "ipred" has bagging(),
which calls rpart().  I have made a "randomForest" package for R, which is
based on Breiman's own Fortran code.  If you set mtry to the number of
predictors in the dataset, randomForest becomes bagging.  For boosting, some
one has also written an R package "LogitBoost" that boost tree stumps.  The
package also relies on rpart.  Do a google search on LogitBoost and you
should find it.

Andy

messages.subject: Re: linear vs. quadratic
messages.body_plain:
You need to define the problem.  Sounds like you have no response variable.  Is 
that right?  If that is not correct, relationships among the predictors are not 
very relevant.  If you do have a single response variable the Design library 
(http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/rms) can help, e.g.

library(Hmisc,T); library(Design,T)
dd <- datadist(mydata)
options(datadist='dd')
# rcs=restricted cublic spline or natural spline
# 4 = # knots, generating 2 nonlinear d.f. per predictor
# (use more or less knots depending on sample size and other things)
# ols = ordinary least squares (or use lrm, cph, psm, glmD, etc.)
f <- ols(y ~ rcs(x1,4)+rcs(x2,4)+rcs(x3,4)+..., data=mydata)
plot(f)  # show all partial effects with confidence bands
anova(f) # test association and get all tests of nonlinearity
         # BUT don't use these tests to simplify the model or
         # statistical properties will be destroyed
         # if you allow for nonlinearity it's usually best to stick with it

If you truly have pairs of variables and don't need a multivariable model you 
can just do the above for one pair at a time, being a little afraid of multiple 
comparison problems.

Frank Harrell

required to obtain the ouput I wanted with manova().  The other two responses
point to or provide code for computing Hotelling's T-squared.

Ted Wright

you could try the following:

# Hotelling's Test
# x is your data in a two columns matrix
n <- dim(x)[1]
p <- dim(x)[2]
x.bar <- as.matrix(colMeans(x))
m0 <- as.matrix(c(0,0))
S <- var(x)
g <-
(n/(n-1))*((n-p)/p)*t(x.bar-m0)%*%solve(S)%*%(x.bar-m0)
p.value <- 1-pf(g, p, n-p)
# Null Hypothesis: x.bar==m0
# Alternative Hypothesis: x.bar!=m0
p.value

I hope this helps.

Best,
Dimitris

messages.subject: read.table() with blank lines
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I'm using S-Plus 6.0.3 under Windows 2000 and S-Plus 2000 under Windows NT.

I'm frequently stymied by read.table() when the file in question has blank 
lines in it. Those blank lines get discarded. I think this is a bug, based on 
the help file's claim that the value returned by read.table() is "a data frame 
with as many rows as the file has lines...". As I say, it omits blank lines 
from the return value, and typically that's not what I want.

For example, consider this:
> tbl <- data.frame (c("Zip", "Zap", "", "Zowie"), c("a", "b", "", "d"))
> tbl
     X1 X2 
1   Zip  a
2   Zap  b
3         
4 Zowie  d

> dim (tbl)
[1] 4 2

So "tbl" is a data.frame with 4 rows. Let's write it out to the clipboard, then 
call read.table().

> write.table (tbl, "clipboard", dimnames.write=F, sep="\t")

> read.table ("clipboard", sep="\t", row.names=NULL)
     V1 V2 
1   Zip  a
2   Zap  b
3 Zowie  d

> dim (read.table ("clipboard", sep="\t", row.names=NULL))
[1] 3 2

That blank line is gone. It's on the clipboard -- I can see that when I paste 
the clipboard somewhere -- but I can't get it back. This means I  run into 
alignment problems if,  for example, two files have the same number of rows, 
only one has blanks where the other doesn't. Then when I read in the two files 
with read.table() the rows don't match up.

What do you think? Bug? Undocumented feature? Whiny user?

Sam ("Blankety-Blank") Buttrey
Man With Blank Lines
buttrey at nps.navy.mil

messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I am a relatively new user of S-Plus so I hope this question is not too simple. 
My question is whether it is possible to do forward stepwise regression using 
generalised additive models. I need to do this because I have many predictors 
(25 or so) and relatively few data points so (~50), so I can't start from the 
full model with all the terms in it and then work backwards. I note that with 
step.glm I can start with the null model and then build it up. 

Regression.start<-glm(Y ~ 1, family=gaussian, na.action=na.omit) 
Regression.step<-step.glm(Regression.start, ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5) 
 
but for the gam model it won't do it: 
 
Regression.start<-gam(Y ~ 1, family=gaussian, na.action=na.omit) 
Regression.step<-step.gam(Regression.start, ~ lo(X1) + lo(X2) + lo(X3) + lo(X4) 
+ lo(X5)) 

Reading through the help it says that the Object needs to contain 
all terms in the scope, so is there anyway to do a stepwise regression, 
term by term starting from the null model, for gam? 

I am using S-Plus 6.0 Professional Release 2 on a Windows 2000 platform.

Thank you for your help
Anthony

messages.body_plain:
Stepwise variable selection may seem to help with your problem but this is 
illusory.  It will only cause more problems.  Without using data reduction 
(that ignores the response variable) you do not have enough observations to 
deal with more than about 3 CANDIDATE variables with 50 observations, if you 
want to get completely reliable results (results that will replicate on future 
observations).

Frank Harrell

messages.subject: Summary: substituting forward slash
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Mr. Dunlap, Prof. Ripley and Mr. Dorai Raj for their help.

I was using sed without single quotes on solaris machine, and
/bin/sh is different in this environment than that of linux.

Detailed mail is attached below.
-Nitin

> On Mon, 12 Aug 2002, Nitin Jain wrote:
>
> > I wish to substitute forward slash in the following vector (temp). I
> > tried:
> >
> > temp<- c(paste(0:7,"/at",sep=""))
> > rename <- function(ss) unix("sed -e s^/^slash^g", ss, out=T)
> > rename(temp)
>
> On Solaris I get:
>    > rename(temp)
>    sh: /: cannot execute
>    sh: slash: not found
>    sh: g: not found
>    character(0)
>    Warning messages:
>      Error exit from shell command "< /tmp/unix847 sed -e s^/^slash^g" in: 
> unix("sed
>            -e s^/^slash^g", ss, out = T)
> and on Linux:
>    > rename(temp)
>    [1] "0slashat" "1slashat" "2slashat" "3slashat" "4slashat" "5slashat" 
> "6slashat"
>    [8] "7slashat"
> This due to differences between /bin/sh on those two systems.
> (On Solaris ^ "cause[s] termination of a word unless quoted",
> just like ;, &, (, ), !, |, <, >, newline, space, and tab.)
>
> I think a general solution is to put single quotes around the
> s^/^slash^g in the sed command.
>
>    > rename <- function(ss) unix("sed -e 's^/^slash^g'", ss, out=T)
>    > rename(temp)
>    [1] "0slashat" "1slashat" "2slashat" "3slashat" "4slashat" "5slashat" 
> "6slashat"
>    [8] "7slashat"
>    > temp
>    [1] "0/at" "1/at" "2/at" "3/at" "4/at" "5/at" "6/at" "7/at"
>

> vector of data by identifying the elements as one of the above:
>
> x is the vector of data I'm trying to subset
>
> trunc <- x/5-floor(x/5)
> subset <- x[trunc==0.2]
>
> Unfortunately, trunc is not exactly equal to 0.2, 0.4 etc as rounding errors
> occur around the 10th decimal.
>
> The same seems to occur if x is either a double precision or integer value.

x/5 is still double precision ...

> Use of the round function doesn't help.

It should: how were you using it?

> Does anyone know a way of getting the answer 0.2 (exactly) to the question
> of 1/5 ?

You can't.  0.2 is not a binary fraction and so cannot be represented
exactly on a binary computer.  That said, I do get

> (1:4)/5 == c(0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8)
[1] T T T T

on S+6.1, but all of them are inexact.  Also, there is all.equal for
testing real numbers, in preference to ==.

However,

        round(x) %% 5

does exactly what you said you were trying to do, protected against
rounding errors in calculating x.

messages.subject: using lme() [summary]
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Dimitris C. Rizopoulos who forwarded some suggestions
pointing to the fact that my model could be overparametrized.

My original question had to do with SINGULAR CONVERGENCE or
FALSE CONVERGENCE message generated by lme with some models.

Basically, I found out that I did not understand well how to
specify random effect when using a dataframe instead of groupedData 
object. In that case, one needs to specify the grouping 
factor (su) with a syntax like:

        random=list(su=pdDiag(~plane-1))

The simpler syntax

        random=pdDiag(~plane-1)

works well only for grouped data object(such as the Machines dataset). 
This is of course explained in Pinheiro & Bates' book but not very
early in the book. 

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

------------------------------------------------------
>From Dimitris C. Rizopoulos:
------------------------------------------------------

Dear Gabriel,

I have dealed with the same kind problems when I tried
to analyze some data!

Dr. Pinheiro and Dr. Lancelot kindly gave me their
suggestions:

Dr. Pinheiro's reply:

The approximate var-cov matrix in question is the one
for parameter estimates, not the random effects. At convergence, the
Hessian matrix of the log-lik is calculated using numerical
differentiation and its  negative
inverse is used to produce confidence intervals in theintervals.lme
method, provided that the resulting matrix is positive-definite. In
principle, if proper convergence was attained, the
Hessian should be negative-definite and, as a result the approx. 
var-cov matrix should be positive-definite. However, in practice 
this may not always be the case, so the code tests for it and issues
the error message.

>From my experience, problems of this sort generally happen when the 
model is overparameterized and the solution is at the boundary of 
the parameter space. Check the estimates for the random effects 
var-cov parameters and try to simplify  the model, if possible.

------------------------------------------------------

Dr. Lancelot's reply:

The first. You can have a look at the matrix to (try
to) see where the problem comes from. Usually, one of the 
terms is very small (e.g. 10-8) and is not properly 
estimated ==> when you remove it, problems are
solved. To get the var-cov matrix, you can use
pdMatrix but results are scales by the residuals variance:

> fm1 <- lme(distance ~ age, data = Orthodont)
> pdMatrix(fm1$modelStruct$reStruct)

.....

To get the "raw" var-cov matrix:

> lapply(pdMatrix(fm1$modelStruct$reStruct), "*", fm1$sigma^2)

...

messages.subject: Optimization Problem
messages.body_plain:
Dear S folks:

Apologies for the question in that it is a more general optimization
problem with hopefully an already existing solution in SPLUS - or at least
a good suggestion on how to tackle it.

Assume I buy and sell 'widgets' for a living.
I can buy them and sell them at some rate (i.e. I can buy a max of 100
widgets a day and sell a max of 50 a day).
My actions of selling and buying can alter the number I have in storage at
any time.
The price of the widgets changes every day and, although I cannot affect
it, I have a clairvoyant way of knowing what it has been , it is now, and
will be in the future.
Given the supply limitations, I would like to sell my widgets 'smartly',
i.e. boost sales during the various price maxima I expect and up my storage
during low price times.

One way I have approached the problem is through dynamic programming
(outside S+) with well optiimized code in terms of programming and
elimination of logically unnecessary steps.  Nevertheless, DP is a very CPU
intensive process and, in my case, prohibitively so.  Is there some other
optimization method you know of (especially one implemented in SPLUS) that
would allow me to do this in a more frugal way?

Thanks for any suggestions you may have,
Yannis Tzamouranis

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all for their helpful suggestions (see below) regarding
working with rows.

Here is what I'm doing:

Suppose "dframe" is the name of the data frame and "last" is the
number of rows.  Make two index vectors of length last*(last-1)/2 to
indicate which row is in which pair.

rows1 <- unlist(lapply(1:last,function(x)rep(x,last-x)))
rows2 <- unlist(lapply(1:last,function(x)seq(x+1,last)))[1:(last*(last-1)/2)]

Then I can cbind the dataframe with itself to get a new data frame,
each row containing a pair of row of the original.

rowpairs <- cbind(dframe[rows1,],dframe[rows2,])

Now everything in all pairs of rows is available for whatever ...

Example:
> dframe <- data.frame(x=1:3,y=6:8,z=10:12)
> dframe
  x y  z 
1 1 6 10
2 2 7 11
3 3 8 12
> last <- dim(dframe)[1]
> last
[1] 3
> rows1 <- unlist(lapply(1:last,function(x)rep(x,last-x)))
> rows1
[1] 1 1 2
> rows2 <- unlist(lapply(1:last,function(x)seq(x+1,last)))[1:(last*(last-1)/2)]
> rows2
[1] 2 3 3
> rowpairs <- cbind(dframe[rows1,],dframe[rows2,])
> rowpairs
    x y  z x1 y2 z3 
 X1 1 6 10  2  7 11
X11 1 6 10  3  8 12
 X2 2 7 11  3  8 12

The second set of column names for are flakey, but so what?

> names(rowpairs)[((dim(rowpairs)[2]/2)+1):dim(rowpairs)[2]] <-
        paste(names(rowpairs)[1:(dim(rowpairs)[2]/2)],"2",sep ="")
+ > 
> rowpairs
    x y  z x2 y2 z2 
 X1 1 6 10  2  7 11
X11 1 6 10  3  8 12
 X2 2 7 11  3  8 12

And the row names can be improved.

> dimnames(rowpairs)[[1]] <- format(1:(last*(last-1)/2))
> rowpairs
  x y  z x2 y2 z2 
1 1 6 10  2  7 11
2 1 6 10  3  8 12
3 2 7 11  3  8 12

* 4301 Rickenbacker Causeway                           *
* Miami, Florida 33149 USA                             *
* Office:  (305) 361-4323                              *
* Fax:     (305) 361-4392                              *

Original question:

Does splus have tools for working with all pairs of rows in a
dataframe?  

For example, dist() acts on pairs of rows to compute distance, but it
gives no information about column values for the rows making up the
pairs.

Is there an easy way to combine a data frame with itself so that each
row of the result will correspond to pairs of rows of the original and
have all of the columns for both members of the pair?  Loops are
pretty slow.
___________________________________________________________________
Sam Buttrey:

Hi. I have no idea if this is slow or not in a big problem, but you
might try this. It works great when your data is a matrix. For a
dataframe this is a harder problem.

> car <- matrix(letters[1:24], nrow=6, byrow=T)  #  my data
> mat <- data.frame (unpaste (outer (1:nrow(car), 1:nrow(car), paste, sep=","), 
> ",")) # get all pairs of integers into a 2-column data frame
> mat [,1] <- as.numeric(mat[,1]) # the columns were characters: make them 
> numeric
> mat[,2] <- as.numeric(mat[,2])
> apply (mat, 1, function(x) cbind (car[x[1],], car[x[2],]))

That gives you what you want, although the answer comes out in columns rather 
than in rows.

When you have a datafra,e the output comes out in a list, which you can "rbind" 
in one call to "do.call":
> car <- data.frame (a = 1:4, b = c("a", "b", "c", "d"))

(create and numeric-i-fy "mat")

> do.call ("rbind", apply (mat, 1, function(x) data.frame (car[x[1],], 
> car[x[2],])))
   a b a1 b2 
 1 1 a  1  a
 2 2 b  1  a
 3 3 c  1  a
 4 4 d  1  a
 5 1 a  2  b
 6 2 b  2  b
 7 3 c  2  b
(etc)
___________________________________________________________________
Peter Alspach
Try something like:

cbind(df[seq(1,(nrow(df)-1),2),], df[seq(2,nrow(df),2),])
___________________________________________________________________
Samantha Low Choy

Perhaps this would provide basis for something useful?

make.pairs <- function(y, include.self=T) {
        n<<-length(y)
        if (include.self) {
                indices <- cbind(
                        unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) {rep(x,n-x+1)} )), 
                        unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) if(x<=n) 
return(seq(x,n))))
                )
        } else {
                indices <- cbind(
                        unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) rep(x,n-x))), 
                        unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) if(x<n) 
return(seq(x+1,n))))
                )
        }
        return(cbind(y[indices[,1]], y[indices[,2]]))
}
make.pairs(c(3,45,3838))

and 

How about using rep(), eg 

        n<-5
        cbind(rep(1:n, n), rep(1:n, rep(n,n)))

This generates every permutation of a pair of numbers in list 1:n.

If you want to randomly select permutations, try using some of the factorial 
design tools to generate indices of pairs? eg fac.design().

If you just want every combination of a pair of numbers in a list 1:n
(ie eliminate repeats in rep() call above), then try using the apply function,
eg all pairs excluding double-ups:

        cbind(
                unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) rep(x,n-x))), 
                unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) if(x<n) return(seq(x+1,n))))
        )

or including double-ups:

        cbind(
                unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) rep(x,n-x+1))), 
                unlist(lapply(1:n, function(x) if(x<=n) return(seq(x,n))))
        )

Hope this helps.
___________________________________________________________________

1    w   10     c     8
2    c    8     b    13
3    b   13     j     4
4    j    4     h     5

messages.subject: Re: character to numeric
messages.body_plain:
The easiest way (I can think of, anyway) is to use awk to extract the data
before reading into Splus.  You didn't say what OS you're using, which
happens to Windoze users the most (they don't seem to realize there *are*
other OSs).  There are several versions of awk under Windoze, e.g., cygwin.

Assuming the files are delimited by white space, you can do something like:

  awk '$1=="I" || $1=="S"' original.data > filtered.data

at the command prompt.  This extracts all rows where the first column are
either "I" or "S" and write them out to the file "filtered.data".  You can
even give awk all the input files at the same time, if you don't need the
output in separate files.

HTH,
Andy

>
> > I have some very large files on my .Data directory (Unix) that start
> > "___"  e.g. "___6oe7".  Can I safely get rid of these?
>
> Yes.  The files in .Data of the form 3 underscores followed by
> some letters and digits are ok to get rid of.  (Those letters
> and digits should be the hexidecimal representation of the
> the process id, perhaps with some trailing stuff, so only 0-9 and
> a-f should be there.)
>
>   Files of the form 2 underscores followed by digits are not ok to
>   get rid of!
>
> The first sort of file is used by Splus to write a dataset into.
> If it is successful writing the entire dataset (there was enough
> space, it wasn't interrupted, there were no permission problems)
> then it renames it to the proper name of the object.  E.g.
>         x <- 1:10
> causes Splus to put 1:10 into the file
>         ___45ac0
> and if that file was completely written without any probems it renames it
>         x
>
> The most common reason for failure to completely write the file is that
> the disk filled up so these orphaned files tend to be large.  They ought
> to be removed when that happens but Splus doesn't remove them now.

messages.subject: Finmetrics Internal Error
messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ers,

I hope someone can help me with an infuriating problem I have.  I am trying to 
model a bivariate GARCH using the Finmetrics module Version 1.0, S+ v6.1 for 
Windoze Professional Trial Edition Release 1.  The explanation is a bit long; 
I've tried to be explicit, since it seems to be an implemenation issue.

The following works fine (either from the command line, or within a function):

"
> len   <-      100
> prices<-      matrix(runif(300), 100, 3)
>
> r     <-      matrix(0, len-1, 3)             
> r     <- apply(log(prices), 2, diff)/1000     # this is 99x3 matrix of log 
> returns, same scale and size as real data
>
> garchOut      <- mgarch(r~ar(1), ~dvec(1, 1), trace=T)        

Iteration   0  Step Size = 0.00235530  Likelihood = -4.97080 
...
Iteration  51  Step Size = 0.00315935  Likelihood = -4.80712 

Convergence R-Square = 0.007055362 
Function value convergence.

> summary(garchOut)
..."

However, when I use the same code with some real prices, the code executes 
silently (from command line, or within a function), but /any/ command line call 
then gives:

"Problem: internal error: trying to set internal exit action in frame 0, must 
be between 1 and 5, while calling subroutine arc
"hresid 
"Use traceback() to see the call stack
"
"Error during wrapup: Invalid frame number (0) in set_frame
"Engine connection failure - shutting down S-PLUS recommended"

And subsequent commands, including traceback() or even q(), give:

"Problem: internal error: trying to set internal exit action in frame 1, must 
be between 1 and 0 
"Use traceback() to see the call stack
"Engine connection failure - shutting down S-PLUS recommended"

The object garchOut doesn't appear in Object Explorer. Closing down S+ then 
leads predictably to an Application Error.  I'm having difficulty locating the 
problem, as I have to restart S+ whenever I try a new avenue.  S+ Univariate 
garch works fine on the same prices data.  Note that the real 'r' is ~0.001.

My guess is that mgarch is generating some warning since 'r' cannot be 
successfully modelled, but that this is having some odd knock-on effect with a 
bug.  Any help would be much appreciated.

Thanks

Robert

At 12:57 PM 8/22/2002 +0400, Arjun Bhandari wrote:

>      -  I tried to use the following set of statements

> of arguments to the function")
>      - Error: No data to interpret as logical value: e1 || e2
>                 - I do not quite understand where I am going wrong.

If I follow correctly what you want to do, you can use missing to check 
whether an argument has been specified; for example,

    > fun <- function(x, y){
    +     if (missing(x) || missing(y)) stop('missing argument')
    +     x + y
    +     }

    > fun(1, 2)
    [1] 3

    > fun(1)
    Problem in fun(1): missing argument
    Use traceback() to see the call stack

On the other hand, if you want your function to take an indefinite number 
of arguments, you can use the dummy argument ... and check  length(c(...)).

> 2.  Matrix division: I want to get the syntax for solving equations AX=B
> and that of XA=B. I get this from matlab but could not find a similar
> function in splus. Would anyone know how to get around this.

Again, if I understand what you want, you can use the solve function to 
solve systems of linear equations; see ?solve.

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.body_plain:
I received several very useful suggestions to my question on translating
multiple, uniquely identified rows from multiple files into one, numeric
Splus file.  I thank Stephen Weller, Andy Liaw, and James Holtman for
their assistance.  I have posted the replies below with the exception of
Stephen Weller's message because he sent it to the list.  At the end of
the replies, I have posted the original message for those interested in
re-reading it.

#----James Holtman---------------
Here is one of doing it.  You read the file in with "scan(...what
='character', sep='\n')" to read in each line as a character vector.
Then separate out the lines that you are interested in in a new object
(in the example below, lines that start with "C").  Then use
'textConnection' to read in this object.

#--------Andy Liaw--------------------------------------------
The easiest way (I can think of, anyway) is to use awk to extract the
data before reading into Splus.  You didn't say what OS you're using,
which happens to Windoze users the most (they don't seem to realize
there *are* other OSs).  There are several versions of awk under
Windoze, e.g., cygwin.

Assuming the files are delimited by white space, you can do something
like:

  awk '$1=="I" || $1=="S"' original.data > filtered.data

at the command prompt.  This extracts all rows where the first column
are either "I" or "S" and write them out to the file "filtered.data".
You can even give awk all the input files at the same time, if you don't
need the output in separate files.

#--------original message-------------------------------------------

> I have multiple data files [ASCII format]. Each file is sequentially 
> numbered and contains a combination of text and numbers.  My interest 
> in the text is only to identify rows. I want the rows that begin with 
> 'I' or 'S'.  There are multiple occurrences of the 'I' and 'S'
> rows in each
> data file.  I want to extract the numbers in those rows that 
> begin with
> 'I' or 'S' for further analysis.  Each row of interest contains 8
> columns of numbers.  I would like to put those columns of numbers in 8
> separate columns of a data frame.  Furthermore, I would like 
> to put in a
> row of "NA" if the row does not exist in the data file.

Respectfully, 
Frank R. Lawrence

messages.subject: Looking for help with lme correlation structure
messages.subject_clean: Looking for help with lme correlation structure
messages.body_plain:
Hi all Splus-gurus,

I'm trying to fit a mixed-effects model with the following structure: I 
have 6 regions, within which I have 90 sites (not exactly 15 per region, 
but close), within each of which I have 2 blocks, within each of which I 
have 3 plots.  For each plot I have a set of diameters of a varying number 
of trees.  I've fit the 3-parameter Weibull function to each of these 
plots, therefore I have three parameters per plot, for a total of 540 
triplets in the structure described above.  I have numerous potential 
predictor variables (eg average height, basal area, etc.) that I'd like to 
use to try to predict these three parameters.

I've constructed a scatterplot matrix of the parameters within the plots, 
which reveals considerable correlation between the parameters (especially 
location and scale).  I'd like to construct a model that includes such a 
correlation structure in the predictive portion.  That is, it's important 
that if I predict a triplet of three parameters for any given plot, that 
the predictions evince something like that correlation structure.  Such a 
correlation structure is not produced from models that predict the three 
parameters separately.

So, what I'd like to do is predict the three parameters simultaneously for 
each plot using the predictor variables and the appropriate random effects, 
including a correlation structure and an appropriate variance structure.  I 
have a model statement like

A.overall <- lme(parameter ~
               TPA * height * ba * model,
                weights=varIdent(form=~1|model),
               correlation = corSymm(form=~1|region/site/block/plot),
               random=~1|region/site/block/plot,
                data=fitbasis)

where model is a 3-level factor distinguishing between the fitted 
parameters of the Weibull distribution (location, shape, and scale).

So, when I fit this model, I get a correlation structure like this:

 Correlation:
       1      2
2 -0.783
3 -0.998  0.767

So, the within-plot residuals have that correlation structure.  Now, how do 
I induce the model to apply that correlation structure to the within-plot 
fitted values?  I guess I want the BLUPS to be correlated in this way 
within the plots.  Can it be done?

Thanks for any and all ideas,

Andrew

messages.subject_clean: Query: Beginer questions on writing functions
messages.body_plain:
At 12:57 PM 8/22/2002 +0400, Arjun Bhandari wrote:

> 1. How does one check if the correct number of arguments have been input.
>      -  I tried to use the following set of statements
>         value<-match.call(expand = F)
>         if((value$y == NULL) || (value$x == NULL)) stop("Incorrect Number
> of arguments to the function")
>      - Error: No data to interpret as logical value: e1 || e2
>                 - I do not quite understand where I am going wrong.

As John Fox pointed out, the simplest way to check for missing arguments is 
the missing() function:

if (missing(x) || missing(y)) stop("Incorrect number of arguments to function")

The reason the expression with ==NULL doesn't work is that x==NULL is not 
the way to test whether x is equal to NULL.  For that, use is.null(x).  The 
expression x==NULL returns a zero-length logical vector (because NULL is a 
zero-length object).

> length(T==NULL)

[1] 0

> mode(T==NULL)

[1] "logical"

> length(c(T,F)==NULL)  # a comparison against a zero-length object always 
returns a zero-length object

[1] 0

> mode(c(T,F)==NULL)

[1] "logical"

PS.  S-plus documentation can be a useful source of information 
(experiencing frustration is a sign that it's time to read it.)  Although 
it does leave something to be desired in terms of organization, it's pretty 
easy to find the section that discusses handling missing arguments: Book: 
"Programmer's Guide to S-plus"; Chapter: 4: Writing functions in S-plus; 
Section: Specifying argument lists; SubSection: Handling Missing Arguments. 
(Page 122 in the S-plus 6 edition dated Jul 2001).

hope this helps,

Tony Plate

messages.subject: print(quote=F) bug in S+ 6.0.3?
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I've found what I think to be a bug in the behavior of print() which shows 
up on a list that includes a data.frame in S+ 6.0.3 release 2 for Windows.

> print (list (a = 1:3))
$a:
[1] 1 2 3 # Works well

> print (list (a = data.frame (1:3)))
$a:
   X1 
1 "1"
2 "2"
3 "3" # not so good

Notice the quotes, which do not appear using the same command in S-Plus 2000. 

I believe the "problem" lies in the fact that the result of format() on a 
data.frame carries class "matrix" in S+ 6.0. print.matrix() doesn't do what you 
would expect here.

Consider this:

> print (matrix ("1"), prefix = "a", quote=T)
     [,1] 
[1,] "1" 
> print (matrix ("1"), prefix = "a", quote=F)  # should have no quote
     [,1] 
[1,] "1" 

I see in print.default() that if the prefix() argument is present we call 
show() instead of the next method for print(). show() then calls print(). 
However, the quote=F argument doesn't propagate to the print() call.

Bug? Feature? User with too much time on his hands?

Slowly losing my mind,
Sam ("Quote = F") Buttrey

messages.body_plain:
Given our experiences with Win98 and Win98SE, we upgraded all our systems 
to Win2000 Pro or WinXP Pro.  We had more than 2 dozen identical machines 
preinstalled with Win98SE.  More than a third of them experienced Windows 
"Shutdown" problems.  After trying every software tweak published on the 
net, replacing motherboards, NIC cards, video cards, memory chips (all at 
the vendor's expense) without ever resolving these problems,  we 
reformatted the hard drives of all those machines with Windows 2000 
Pro.  Interestingly enough, the problems never occurred again.  This 
experience led me to conclude that Windows 98SE (in particular) was one of 
Microsoft's least stable OSes.

That Insightful considers this particular problem intractable for Win98 
comes as no surprise.

messages.body_plain:
Hi. I am a Masters student 
preparing to defend my thesis. I have come up with a problem I am not sure how 
to address. I am performing logistic regression on my data based on a 
dichotomous disease outcome (yes/no). I am worried that there might be a 
correlation between two of my variables (one is nights awake per month, and the 
other is use of a supplemental hormome). I did a Point Beserial Correlation and 
got and R of 0.15, that was signficant. This was sucha small number, I assumed 
the correlation was weak. However, it was then suggested to me to do a simple 
t-test comparing the mean of nights for the two yes/no groups and doing so, I 
get significant differences, with one group having a mean twice that of the 
other, which to me implies correlation. Do you know the best way to sort this 
out? I am unsure which is most correct. Thanks.

messages.subject_clean: Functions from R, and (the lack) of Noncentral Capability
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I was wondering if it would be possible to use R's pt() function in 
place of the pt() function in S-Plus?  Unfortunately S-Plus does not 
allow for a noncentral parameter in determining t probabilities from 
noncentral distributions.  I've heard that pasting some functions into 
S-Plus from R works fine, but, in the case of pt() it doesn't.  

Also, more for the Insightful people, is there any likelihood that a 
function for pt() with a noncentrality parameter and especially a qt() 
with a noncentrality parameter will be developed anytime soon?  As of 
right now I feel that biggest "thing" that is missing from S-Plus is the 
lack of noncentrality capability.  I realize the pchisq() and pf() allow 
for noncentral parameters, but, neither of these allow for noncentral 
parameters for the finding quantiles.  It is frustrating because I try 
to use S-Plus for all of my work, but, I am increasingly working with 
noncentral distributions, which forces me to use SAS or other programs 
when better noncentral capabilities.

Thanks very much,
Ken

Shayna Padgett <shayna at knology.net> wrote:

> Hi. I am a Masters student preparing to defend my thesis. I have come up with 
> a problem I am not sure how to address. I am performing logistic regression 
> on my data based on a dichotomous disease outcome (yes/no). I am worried that 
> there might be a correlation between two of my variables (one is nights awake

Let the multivariable logistic regression do its job and estimate the partial 
effects (odds ratios or log odds ratios) of interest.  You need not worry about 
correlations among the predictors unless there is strong collinearity.  I 
suggest working through a logistic regression text.  You do not need to be 
looking at point biserial correlations and t-tests in my opinion.

messages.subject: lme questions
messages.body_plain:
Can somebody help me with a couple of questions about lme() syntax
for a model with an interaction term without the main effect and 
about how to fit various heteroscedastic models in which variance 
depend additively from the levels of two factors [SP2000]. I will
post a summary of the answers (Is there still a lme-help list?).

In an experiment about the perception of orientations,
Eight subjects were shown a stimulus in one of four orientations (0, 
45, 90 or 138 deg) and asked to reproduce it. Each orientation was 
presented 6 times to each subject in a randomized order. For each 
trial, I recorded the error (angular difference between true and
reproduced orientation) made by the subject. There were two
outliers that are not included in the analysis.

        8 subjects (i=1,..,8)
        4 orientations (j=1,..,4) 
        5 or 6 replicates (k=1,..5 or 6).

The linear mixed-effects model is

        yijk~mu + aj + bi + bij + eijk

where aj is a fixed effect representing the effect of the orientation
      bi is a random effect representing a general tendency of
         the ith subject to overestimate or underestimate the true
         orientation
      bij is a random effect representating the subject by orientation
         interaction.

A look at the data suggests the following about the random effects

      1) bi could be removed from the model because subjects
         do not overstimate or under estimate all orientations

         => Var(bi)~ 0 

      2) the interaction plot show that that the erreors depend both on 
         the orientation and on the subject. Interestingly, all subjects
         are more accurate for the 90 degree orientation (i.e. the
         systematic errors are smaller for the 90 degree orientation) 
         which suggests the following structure for the bij term

         => var(bij) = diag(sb.1,sb.2,sb.3,sb.4)                     [2.a]
          or 
         => var(bij) = diag(sb.1,sb.1,sb.3,sb.1) with sb.3 small     [2.b]

      3) some subjects are in general more consistent than others
     
         => var(eijk) = s.i  with s.i different for each subjec        [3]

      4) all subjects are more consistent for the 90 degree orientation
         (i.e. the variable error for the 90 degree orientation is small)

          => var(eijk) = s.j with s.j different for each orientation   [4]

      5) observations 3 and 4 together suggest

          => var(eijk) = s1.i + s2.j                                   [5]

The following syntax (plane is a factor coding the orientation and 
grp codes the combination between su and plane)

        aux$grp<-factor(paste(aux$su,aux$plane))
 
        fit<-lme(response~plane,random=list(grp=pdDiag(form=~plane-1)),
                weights=varIdent(form=~1|su),
                data=aux)

defines (see below) var(bij) as in [2.a] and var(eijk) as in [3]. If 
the weights statement is

        weights=varIdent(form~1|plane)

then var(eijk) is defined as in [4].

Questions:

        1) I am not sure about the blocking factor for the random effets
          bij. Both
          
                random=list(grp=pdDiag(form=~plane-1))
           and
                random=list(su=pdDiag(form=~plane-1))

        yields four estimates of the variance parameters related to bij. 
       Estimates are similar but not exactly equal. In addition, there 
       are several differences. In the first case, ranef(fit) yields 
       a 32 by 4 matrix with one non-zero value per row while it 
       yields a 8 by 4 matrix in the second case. Besides, 
       anova(fit) yields a test for the fixed effects with 28 df 
       for the denominator in the first case and 179 df in the second 
       case. The first syntax defines 32 groups while the second 
       syntax defines only 8 groups. To me, the first syntax is 
       more correct since bij models the interaction. However, the 
       plot of the random effects qqnrom(fit,~ranef(.)) looks wrong 
       when grp is used as the  blocking factor because of the many 
       zeros.

       Note that the syntax is straightforward if the main
       effect bi is included in the model:

          random=list(su=~1,plane=pdDiag(form=~plane-1))

        2) What is the syntax for [2.b] ?

        3) What is the syntax for [5] ?

I have tried 

        weights=varComb(varIdent(form=~1|plane),varIdent(form=~1|su))   [6]

but this defines var(eijk) = s1.i*s2.j (i.e., multiplication of the
variances).

I have tried 

        weights=varIdent(form=~1|plane*su)                              [7]

but this defines var(eijk) = s.ij (different variance for each combination
of subject and orientation => 32 parameters!).

Note that when I fitted these different models, the likelihood ratio test
indicated that the fit of [6] or [7] was significantly better than the 
fit of [3] or [4]. Likelihood ratio tests favored model [3] or [4] over
a model assuming homeoscedasticity (i.e. var(eijk) = s). Although I could
use [6] or [7], I would prefer a model where the variance are added
rather than multiplied and with less parameters to be estimated 
than model [7].

If one were to define a new varFunc to implement [5], what functions 
would need to be implemented? Pinheiro and Bates write  (p. 214) that 
one must write a constructor and, at minimum, methods for the 
functions coef, coef<- and initialize. I have looked at the manner in 
which these functions are implemented for varComb and none of them 
seem sto carry out the multiplication. However, varWeights.varComb()  
multiplies the weights. This leads me to wonder which function 
does actually carry out the multiplication when the model is fitted? 
If it is varWeights.varComb, does that mean that I would have to 
change this function into something like

varWeights.varCombSum<-function(object)
{
        apply(as.data.frame(lapply(object, varWeights)), 1, 
                function(x) 1/sum(1/x))
}

Thank you for your help

Gabriel

messages.subject_clean: magnitude of response variable and AIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to model activity data against weather 
variables in S-PLUS 2000 using AIC as a model selection 
criterion....

 

The range of the response variable is 0 - 850,000 
and is poisson-like in distribution.  I am using a poisson family GLM to do 
this.  The AIC values of these models are huge ( in the millions).  
Therefore what tends to happen when you are ranking different models via the 
Akaike weights is that the best model is ranked as one (of course), and because 
the actual magnitude of the difference between the first and second best is in 
the thousands it gets an Akaike weight of essentially 0 and therefore all other 
candidate models become ranked as tied for second best.  This seemed 
odd..

I experimented with transforming the response 
variable by dividing by 100,000.  What I am finding is that the values of 
the AIC are now in the order to 100 or so and the ranking the models via Akaike 
weights appears to be ok.

HOWEVER, when I rank the models using both 
approaches from lowest to highest AIC values they are not the same-- The AIC 
selected best models were different, WHY??.

 

Can anyone provide insight into why 
this occurs.

Thanks in advance

messages.subject: lme question shortened
messages.body_plain:
I have posted some questions about the mixed model approach for
a repeated-measure design last week. The post was probably too 
long for most people. I can summarize the previous post into 
two short questions. I would greatly appreciate your comments 
and I'll post a summary of the responses.

1) how to use lme() when the random effect is not statistically
significant but the interaction between the fixed and random
factors is significant?

2) how to use lme() when the residual variance depends in an 
ADDITIVE manner from the levels of the fixed effect AND from 
the levels of the random effect?

I give a little bit more of details and motive these questions
below.  Let assume that I have a repeated measures design with 
eight subjects (su factor) who perform a task in four different 
conditions (plane factor). Each conditon is presented six times 
to each subject in a randomized order (6 replications). 

1) With respect to the first question, the most common examples 
involving an interaction I have seen in books were modeled
with a two-level random effects model:

lme(response~plane,random=~1|su/plane,data) 

but what if var(su)~0 and I would like to simplify
the model ? One possibility is:

data$grp<-factor(paste(data$su,data$plane)
lme(response~plane,random=~1|grp,data)

In that case, is the following correct

lme(response~plane,random=list(grp=pdDiag(form=~plane)),data)

if the variance depends on the level of plane? A LRT test
with my dataset shows marked improvement with respect to the 
previous model but there are many zeros in ranefs() and the 
corresponding qqnorm plots look strange because of these zeros.

2) With respect to the second questions. I know two methods
with the weights argument:

        weights=varComb(varIdent(form=~1|plane),varIdent(form=~1|su))
or
        weights=varIdent(form=~1|plane*su)           

but the first one multiplies and not add the variances and the
second one define a parameters for each combination of levels. I
have looked at the varComb function as a guide to program a new 
set of functions to implement the desired behavior but I could not 
find which function actually carries out the multiplication of 
the variance during the fit of the model. 

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

messages.body_plain:
The second argument to do.call() is a *list of arguments* to the function, 
and a data frame is a list.  So, when you do do.call('boxplot', dataframe) 
or do.call("boxplot", as.list(dataframe)), boxplot gets called with 
multiple arguments: the columns of the data frame.  But, when you do 
do.call("boxplot", list(dataframe)), boxplot gets just one argument: the 
dataframe.

Easily verified:

> foo <- function(...) browser()
> do.call("foo", data.frame(a=1:3,b=4:6))

messages.subject: Summary: Subtleties of classes methods
messages.body_plain:
My thanks to Tony Plate and Bill Dunlap who, between them, mostly resoved my
confusion. It has nothing to do with classes, but rather that:

a) boxplot is not properly documented in the Help file (again, poor
documentation !)
b) I was not smart enough to look at the boxplot generic and see that it
needed an "x" argument and thereby figure out (at least partially) for
myself what the issue was.

Here are the details, synthesized from their two replies.

If z is a data.frame, it already is a list. Therefore, as.list(z) = z . So
if z has 10 named components, so does as.list(z). In other words, as.list()
does nothing here.

However, list(z) is a list with one unnamed component, the list, z.

Now do.call's 2nd argument should be a list.Therefore:

>do.call ('boxplot',z) calls the generic function boxplot, with arguments
the NAMED components of z. None of these components is named 'x', which is
what the generic needs to be supplied, either implicitly or explicitly
(except that it can't be done explicitly -- see below).

However,
>do.call('boxplot',list(z)) calls boxplot with argument one UNNAMED
component, z. Now here's where things get weirder. This is the same as 
>boxplot(z) and boxplots the data properly for z a data.frame or a list (as
the default method takes care of lists). 
Therefore, one would think that 

>boxplot(x=z) would work, but it doesn't -- the error "Error in boxplot: no
data" bubbles up from the Fortran code.. 

Even cuter, 
>boxplot(x=list(),z)  or >boxplot(x=1:3,z)
Both produce the plots but then choke while trying to title them and bubble
up interesting Fortran error messages. I can do no better then to quote Bill
Dunlap's reply to this "feature" :

*** BILL DUNLAP REPLY ****
I don't have a good answer for this now, but
boxplot has acted this way since at least Splus3.3.
It looks like if you name the first argument (x=something)
then it throws it away (and complains about "no data")!

It got a little more confused when boxplot was made into
a generic function.  Before then it had no x= argument and
now it does.

*************
So that's it for now, folks. None of this is documented, of course
(especially the fact that boxplot() is now a generic), so I am grateful for

messages.subject: buggy boxplot()
messages.body_plain:
All:

Following up on my post to the list yesterday and Bill Dunlap's comment
regarding boxplot(), I wanted to let all know that boxplot()  is partially
broken, is unlikely to be fixed (Bill said it's been broken for years), and
is not documented (SFAIK). Below is what I have found about the nature of
the problem in fooling around a bit. Fortunately, the workaround is simple:
DO NOT USE NAMED ARGUMENTS in the form name=arg IN THE ... ARGUMENTS OF
BOXPLOT. It should work fine if you adhere to this. (An unnamed list with
named components given as the argument works fine. That is,
boxplot(list(x=1:10)) works fine, but neither boxplot(x=1:10) nor boxplot
(x=list(1:10)) do  ).

Examples: (S-Plus 6.1 under WINNT)

Single argument:
> boxplot(1:10)  works
> boxplot(x=1:10)  doesn't  (Fortran "no data" error)
> boxplot(y=1:10) doesn't (S-Plus "argument 'x' is missing" error)

 Multiple arguments
>boxplot(1:10,1:10)  works
>boxplot(x=1:10,1:10) gives one boxplot and then  Fortran error messages:
"Can't change integer to character" and "Error in title"
>boxplot(1:10,x=1:10) is the same as previous

>boxplot(1:10,y=1:10) and boxplot(y=1:10,1:10) both start a graph that is
wrong and then give a bunch of "line out of bounds" warnings before ending
with junk.

>boxplot(x=1:10,y=1:10) and boxplot(y=1:10,x=1:10)   both give the Fortran
"no data" error.

Obviously, if these are not bugs and if there's something here that I just
don't get, please let me know.

Cheers,

includes a gaussian frailty, e.g.

messages.subject: modelling a nested MANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Hello.  I am trying to analyse a data set with 
multiple dependent variables in a nested design.  This requires a nested 
MANOVA and I don't know how to specify the error structure.  I am using 
SPLUS 6.  Any help is welcome.

Data structure:  A field is divided into 4 
blocks.  Each block contains 4 parcels and one of 4 levels of a treatment 
is randomly assigned to each parcel in each block.  6 soil cores are 
randomly extracted from each parcel and each soil core is analysed in 
triplicate.  There are 26 dependent variables (abundances of each of 26 
"species" of soil bacteria).  

 

Analysis: Because of the nested structure, the 
treatment effect has to compare the responses between treatments with the 
responses between parcels within  treatments (similarly for the block 
effect).  Systematic differences between soil cores within a parcel would 
be tested by comparing the between-cores within parcels responses to the 
between-replicates within cores within parcels responses.

 

Model (I think...): cbind(y1,y2 etc) ~ block + 
treatment + block:treatment + cores%in%block:treatment

 

Problem:

How do I specify that the treatment and block 
effects are to be tested using the block:treatment term as the error and not the 
default residuals (which are the between-replicates within cores within 
parcels)?

messages.subject_clean: problem computing dfbeta by residuals.coxph in model with a cluster term
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Terry Therneau for a rapid and effective solution to the problem
of computing a dfbeta residual.  He notes that the problem probably results
from an error when the residual function tries to reconstruct the design
matrix for the model.  This problem can be avoided if one includes an
"x=TRUE" argument to the coxph function call:

        coxph(formula = Surv(start, stop, event) ~ C(trt, plac.ref) +
not.first + cluster(pid), data = chfc.wei, x=TRUE)

This causes the coxph function to store a copy of the design matrix (as "x")
in the model object.  The residuals.coxph function then computes the dfbeta
residuals correctly.

Thanks again, Terry.

Larry Hunsicker

messages.subject: Re: Bug in the Print command
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tristan,

This isn't a bug, but reflects the way that print methods are supposed to 
work -- in addition to printing an object they return the object invisibly. 
When you call print at the command line, you don't see the invisible 
result, but the result is returned by print and will be returned by your 
function if it is in the last statement of the function, and then printed 
if not assigned.

For example:

    > fun <- function(x) print(x)
    > fun(1)
    [1] 1
    [1] 1

    > x <- print(1)
    [1] 1
    > x
    [1] 1
    >

I hope that this helps,
 John

Any help with the code for the random factor for a single measurement and

messages.subject: extracting data vector from multiple Excel files
messages.subject_clean: extracting data vector from multiple Excel files
messages.body_plain:
My dataset of accounting data on 110,000 companies has its primary existence
in the form of Excel spreadsheets.

Each year's data  is stored in a directory containing 13 spreadsheet files
(with columns for each of 105 variables) corresponding to the one-digit SIC
code applicable to the company, with supplementary files where the number of
firms under a given one-digit code exceeds the maximum number of rows
allowed in Excel.

Thus, obtaining an S+ vector for a given variable for a given year involves
extracting the relevant column from each spreadsheet and concatenating the
results.

A function on the following lines is intended to do this:

make.my.data <- function(date, data=c("foo", "bar", ...)){
        
        # where "foo", "bar" are variable names (I only need approx. 20
variables from the total available)

        data <- match.arg(data)

        switch(data,
                foo = {data.col <- 53},
                bar = {data.col <- 48}.
                ...)#

        # in order to set TargetStartCol, EndCol = data.col
        
        switch(data,
                foo = {data.mode <- "numeric"},
                bar = {data.mode <- "character"},
                ...)#
        
        # sets data.mode [= "numeric" for most]
        

        import.data(DataFrame = "temp",
                FileName=
                        paste("C:\\  ... [drills down through possibly
over-complex directory structure ] ... \\19", date, "\\0-", date, ".xls",
sep=""),
                FileType="EXCEL",
                TargetStartCol=data.col, EndCol=data.col,
                NameRow=1)
        guiClose("data.frame", "temp")

        temp.0 <- as.vector(temp, mode = data.mode)

        # ...

        import.data(DataFrame = "temp",
                FileName=
                        paste("C:\\Data\\Data sets\\From
Roberto\\Data97xl\\Excel files\\19", date, "\\9-", date, ".xls", sep=""),
                FileType="EXCEL",
                TargetStartCol=data.col, EndCol=data.col,
                NameRow=1)
        guiClose("data.frame", "year")

        temp.9 <- as.vector(temp)

        rm(temp)

        output <- rbind(temp.0, temp.1, temp.2, temp.3, temp.4, temp.5,
temp.6a, temp.6b, temp.7, temp.8a, temp.8b, temp.8c, temp.9)
}

This seems to work OK if one confines oneself to extracting only a few of
the SIC code sections, but trying this out (for a numeric variable) on the
full set crashes S+ -- apparently after about five sections.

(S+ 2k Professional, on a Wintel box -- Pentium Pro with 265MB of RAM; speed
escapes me).

FWIW, the resulting error message is:

SPLUS caused an invalid page fault in
module SAPIOBJ.DLL at 0137:00e88471.
Registers:
EAX=00000000 CS=0137 EIP=00e88471 EFLGS=00010286
EBX=00000000 SS=013f ESP=0110bf5c EBP=0110bf60
ECX=ffffffff DS=013f ESI=029a4980 FS=0cff
EDX=ffffffff ES=013f EDI=027cbbfc GS=0000
Bytes at CS:EIP:
0f be 08 85 c9 74 2f 8b 55 fc d1 e2 89 55 fc 8b 
Stack dump:
00000000 0110bf78 00e88403 00000000 00000000 ffffffff 00000000 0110bfb4
00e87efa 00000000 0110bfac 0110bfa8 0284b96c 00002a9d 00002a9c 00000004 

A version which rbinds the dataframes before coercing them to vectors
suffers a similar fate.

Can anyone explain this behaviour and/or suggest a better approach?

The Open University

Milton Keynes
MK7 6AA
United Kingdom
+44 1908 654658

messages.subject: boxplot order ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all, 
I am making boxplots of numerous variables using months as the grouping factor 
(months here is indeed a factor). I am using gui plots as opposed to command 
line only for their greater flexibility. 

The problem I'm running into is that the boxplots (which plot numerically 
correctly) are produced in alphabetical order, which pretty much kills their 
utility as monthly groupings  :). 

I reviewd all of the "box" functions (command and gui) and didn't find anyway 
to control the order of placement. I thought of trying months() to force 
somekind of internal order, so I tried months() on my timeDate field, and 
voila! perfect ordering. 

So, my question is kind of general... how can I coerce a placement order for 
boxplots, etc. when an internal ordering (such as months) is not appropriate or 
available. Lets say I have three factors, B, S, and V. If I plot those up, they 
will plot in that (alphabetic) order. But say the correct order for my purposes 
is actually S,V,B (or whatever)...

I see that 

is.factor(months(mydata$timeDate))
[1] T

but beyond that I do not understand how months() sets up the ordering, because 

> months()

yields no info. I guess this is an internal method, or function that is not 
visible??

My original "months" column is also a factor, with the exception that under 
"Properties", the order ("Apr", "Aug" , "Dec"...)  is alphabetical, as opposed 
to calendrical (new word ? :):).  The coerced months factor (which works 
correctly) has the order ("Jan", "Feb", "Mar" ...) under "Properties". I tried 
copying this order into the factor "Properties" of the original months", and 
hosed the order really well. I think it offset the order by some number; 
obviously bad (but not understood).

I'm Running 6.0 R2 on windows 2K @ 87 octane

Any ideas are greatly appreciated. 

regards

Michael Slattery
Geologist, Ohio EPA
Columbus OH 43215
614-728-1221 (Ph)
614-644-2909 (Fax)
michael.slattery at epa.state.oh.us

for me:

>       I had run into a similar problem recently.  The solution (with a

>.First <- function()   
>       {
>       ## ---------------------------------------
>       ## Change time.out.format option to import

>       ## ---------------------------------------

>       }
